introduction_markdown: Answer ALL questions. Section I is designed to be answered in 1 hour and Section II in 1½ hours. You are advised to divide your time accordingly. In Section II answer EITHER parts a, b and c OR parts d, e and f of each question (Section II: answer ALL questions, choosing one question from each pair of alternatives). For your guidance the approximate mark for each part of a question is indicated in brackets. You are reminded of the necessity for good English and orderly presentation in your answers. In calculations you are advised to show all the steps in your working, giving your answer at each stage. Where necessary, assume: the acceleration of free fall, $g = 10\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}$; the speed of light in air, $c = 3\times10^{8}\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$; the charge on an electron, $e = 1.6\times10^{-19}\,\mathrm{C}$. Calculators are allowed.

questions.enonce_markdown:
(i) Sketch a displacement-distance graph for two cycles of a wave profile. On it, indicate the amplitude and the wavelength of the wave. *[3 marks]*

(ii) Describe an experiment to determine the speed of sound in air. Your description should include:

- a labelled diagram
- the procedure followed in collecting data
- the processing of the data to determine the speed of sound
- any precaution taken to minimise error. *[7 marks]*
questions.corrige_markdown:
(i) **Graph:** draw the horizontal axis as *distance* (along the direction of travel) and the vertical axis as *displacement*. The curve is a smooth sine wave through the origin: it rises to a crest of height $+A$ at a quarter of the cycle, returns to zero at half of the cycle, falls to a trough of $-A$ at three quarters, and returns to zero at the end of the first wavelength $\lambda$. The same shape is repeated for the second cycle, so the curve ends at a distance $2\lambda$.

- **Amplitude $A$:** the maximum displacement from the equilibrium (zero) line, marked from the axis to the top of a crest.
- **Wavelength $\lambda$:** the distance between two successive crests (or two successive troughs), marked along the distance axis.

(ii) **Echo method.**

**Apparatus and labelled diagram:** a trundle wheel or long tape measure, a stopwatch, two wooden blocks (or a hand clapper), and a large, tall, flat wall (or cliff). Diagram: the observer stands holding the stopwatch and the blocks at a measured distance $d$ from the wall; an arrow marked "sound" goes from the observer to the wall and a second arrow marked "echo" comes back; the distance $d$ is labelled.

**Procedure:** measure the distance $d$ from the observer to the wall (about $100\,\mathrm{m}$). Clap the blocks together and start the stopwatch at the same instant; stop the stopwatch when the echo is heard. Repeat several times (and, if possible, for other distances) and record the times $t$ in a table.

**Processing of the data:** the sound travels to the wall and back, a distance $2d$, in time $t$. Find the mean time $\bar t$ and calculate $v = \dfrac{2d}{\bar t}$. (Alternatively plot a graph of $2d$ against $t$ for several distances; the gradient is the speed of sound.)

**Precautions:** stand far enough from the wall (at least $50\,\mathrm{m}$) so that the echo time is long compared with the reaction time and the echo is heard separately from the clap; use a large flat wall; measure the distance carefully; repeat the timing and take the average; start the watch at the instant of the clap and not at the movement of the hands; do the experiment on a calm day away from other noises.

questions.enonce_markdown:
A ship's sonar sends down a sound of frequency $6000\,\mathrm{Hz}$ into water in a sea, at a point which is $3000\,\mathrm{m}$ deep. The echo is heard $4$ seconds later.

(i) Which wave phenomenon is responsible for echoes? *[1 mark]*

(ii) Calculate the speed of the sound in water. *[2 marks]*

(iii) Calculate the wavelength of the sound. *[2 marks]*

(iv) State a factor which affects the speed of the sound in water. *[1 mark]*
questions.corrige_markdown:
(i) **Reflection** of the sound wave at the sea bed.

(ii) The sound goes down and comes back, so the distance travelled is $2\times 3000 = 6000\,\mathrm{m}$ in $4\,\mathrm{s}$:

$v = \dfrac{\text{distance}}{\text{time}} = \dfrac{6000}{4} = 1500\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$.

(iii) $\lambda = \dfrac{v}{f} = \dfrac{1500}{6000} = 0.25\,\mathrm{m}$.

(iv) The temperature of the water (also its salinity, or its pressure/density).

questions.enonce_markdown:
A boy stands $100\,\mathrm{cm}$ in front of a large plane mirror and observes the image of a girl who is standing $50\,\mathrm{cm}$ behind him.

(i) How far is the image of the girl seen in the mirror from the boy? *[3 marks]*

(ii) State one property of the image. *[1 mark]*
questions.corrige_markdown:
(i) The girl is $50\,\mathrm{cm}$ behind the boy, so her distance from the mirror is $100 + 50 = 150\,\mathrm{cm}$. A plane mirror forms the image as far behind the mirror as the object is in front of it, so the image is $150\,\mathrm{cm}$ behind the mirror.

Distance from the boy to the image $= 100 + 150 = 250\,\mathrm{cm} = 2.5\,\mathrm{m}$.

(ii) The image is **virtual** (it cannot be formed on a screen). Other properties: upright, the same size as the object, laterally inverted, and as far behind the mirror as the object is in front of it. (Any one.)

questions.enonce_markdown:
(i) Draw a ray diagram of a convex lens to show how rays parallel to the principal axis and passing through it are refracted. On the diagram, indicate the principal focus and the focal length. *[3 marks]*

(ii) Describe an experiment to determine the focal length of a convex lens using the plane mirror method. Your description should include:

- a labelled diagram
- the procedure followed in collecting data
- the processing of the data to determine the focal length
- any precaution taken to minimise error. *[7 marks]*
questions.corrige_markdown:
(i) **Ray diagram.** Draw the lens as a double-convex shape with the principal axis through its centre (the optical centre $C$). Draw a ray from the left parallel to the principal axis: on passing through the lens it is refracted and **passes through the principal focus $F$** on the right of the lens. Draw a second ray passing through the optical centre $C$ of the lens: it goes straight through **undeviated**. Mark $F$ on the principal axis where the refracted ray crosses it, and mark the **focal length $f$** as the distance $CF$ from the optical centre to the principal focus. Put arrows on all rays.

(ii) **Plane mirror method.**

**Apparatus and labelled diagram:** an illuminated object (a lamp box with cross-wires in a hole in a screen), a convex lens in a holder, a small plane mirror placed behind the lens (flat against the lens holder, perpendicular to the principal axis), a metre rule. Diagram: from left to right, the cross-wire object (lamp), the lens, then the plane mirror; the principal axis is drawn through the centres and the distance $f$ between the lens and the cross-wires is labelled.

**Procedure:** place the lens and the plane mirror in a line with the cross-wire object on the principal axis. Move the lens (with the mirror behind it) towards or away from the object until a sharp, inverted image of the cross-wires is focussed on the screen beside the object itself, the image and the object being the same size. When this happens, the rays leaving the lens are parallel and fall normally on the mirror, so they return along their own path. Measure the distance $f$ from the object (cross-wires) to the lens with the metre rule. Repeat several times and record the values in a table.

**Processing of the data:** at the position of the sharp image, the cross-wires are at the principal focus of the lens, so the focal length is the measured distance. Calculate the mean of the readings: $f = \dfrac{f_1 + f_2 + f_3 + \dots}{n}$.

**Precautions:** make sure the mirror is perpendicular to the principal axis and the object, lens and mirror are all centred on the axis; work in a darkened room so that the image is easy to see; judge the sharpest image carefully; measure from the optical centre of the lens, with the eye vertically above the scale to avoid parallax; repeat and average.

questions.enonce_markdown:
Figure 2 shows two rays diverging from a stone, O, at the bottom of a $1\,\mathrm{m}$ deep pond. The refractive index of water is $1.3$.

![fig-1](gce-ol-physics-2021-p2-officiel-cameroun_exercice_7_fig_1.png)

*Figure 2*

(i) Define refractive index. *[1 mark]*

(ii) Calculate the apparent depth of the stone to an observer. *[2 marks]*

(iii) What wave phenomenon is responsible for the change in direction of the light as it moves into air? *[1 mark]*

(iv) Given that the speed of light in air is $3.0\times10^{8}\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$, determine the speed of light in water. *[2 marks]*
questions.corrige_markdown:
(i) The **refractive index** $n$ of a medium is the ratio of the sine of the angle of incidence (in air) to the sine of the angle of refraction (in the medium) for light passing from air into that medium: $n = \dfrac{\sin i}{\sin r}$. Equivalently, it is the ratio of the speed of light in air to the speed of light in the medium, $n = \dfrac{c}{v}$.

(ii) $n = \dfrac{\text{real depth}}{\text{apparent depth}}$, so

apparent depth $= \dfrac{\text{real depth}}{n} = \dfrac{1}{1.3} = 0.77\,\mathrm{m}$.

The stone appears to be about $0.77\,\mathrm{m}$ below the surface (at the point I of the figure, where the dotted back-extension of the oblique ray meets the vertical ray).

(iii) **Refraction**: light changes speed when it passes from water into air, so the oblique ray is bent away from the normal.

(iv) $n = \dfrac{c}{v_w}$, so $v_w = \dfrac{c}{n} = \dfrac{3.0\times10^{8}}{1.3} = 2.3\times10^{8}\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$.

questions.enonce_markdown:
On a stormy day, a student sees lightning in the cloud and hears the sound $20$ seconds later.

(i) Explain why he sees the lightning before hearing the sound. *[1 mark]*

(ii) Given that the speed of sound in air is $340\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$, determine how far from the student was the cloud producing the lightning. *[2 marks]*

(iii) State one factor which affects the speed of sound in air. *[1 mark]*
questions.corrige_markdown:
(i) Light travels much faster ($3\times10^{8}\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$) than sound ($340\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$ in air), so the light reaches the student almost instantly, while the sound takes several seconds to arrive.

(ii) The time taken by light is negligible, so the sound travels the whole distance in $20\,\mathrm{s}$:

$d = vt = 340\times 20 = 6800\,\mathrm{m} = 6.8\,\mathrm{km}$.

(iii) The temperature of the air (the speed increases as the temperature rises). Other factors: humidity, wind.
